definition: A friendly king, queen, or tribe that agrees to stay at peace and help another power.
A large oval Roman arena with stone seats where crowds watched gladiator fights and wild animal shows.
A stone channel or bridge built by Roman engineers to carry fresh spring water into towns and bathhouses.
A history detective who carefully digs up ancient buildings, coins, bones, and pottery buried in the ground.
A non-citizen soldier from across the Roman Empire who earned Roman citizenship after twenty-five years of service.
The Latin word for a Roman army fort, surviving today inside British city names ending in -chester or -caster.
A fast, two-wheeled wooden war cart pulled by ponies and ridden into battle by Celtic leaders like Boudicca.
A buried band of scorched red clay, black ash, and melted pots left where an ancient town burned down.
Wise Celtic priests, judges, and teachers who memorised sacred laws and prayers instead of writing books.
The supreme ruler of the vast Roman Empire, commanding all Roman armies, governors, and provinces.
The busy open-air marketplace and public meeting square right in the middle of a Roman town.
The guarded border line at the edge of an empire separating Roman territory from unconquered lands beyond.
An Iron Age hilltop settlement ringed with steep earth ramparts, deep ditches, and wooden fences for protection.
A secret collection of valuable coins, silver spoons, or jewellery buried underground to keep it safe from raiders.
Roman underfloor central heating where hot air from a wood furnace flowed between brick pillars beneath the floor.
The language spoken and written by the Romans, which gave us our ABC alphabet and thousands of English words.
Something important handed down from the past, such as roads, cities, calendars, or words that still shape life today.
A full-time, heavily armoured Roman citizen soldier trained to march twenty miles a day and fight in tight formations.
A small stone fortlet and guarded gateway built at every single Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A colourful Roman floor picture made by pressing thousands of tiny cut stone cubes called tesserae into mortar.
A conquered country or region outside Italy ruled by a Roman governor who collected Roman taxes.
An armed uprising where angry people fight back to overthrow the rulers controlling them.
The Roman way of writing numbers using capital letters such as I for one, V for five, and X for ten.
A circular Celtic family home with woven clay walls, a central hearth fire, and a tall thatched roof without a chimney.
A tall, curved rectangular Roman shield made of layered wood, leather, and a central iron boss.
The Latin word for tortoise, naming the battle formation where soldiers locked shields in front and overhead against arrows.
A heavy, twisted neck ring crafted from gold, silver, or bronze and worn by wealthy Celtic leaders.
A grand Roman stone country house built for wealthy landowners, often decorated with mosaic floors and underfloor heating.
